content:
Key Takeaways

  • FD rates at major Indian banks now range from 6.45% to 6.80%. After tax in the 30% bracket, that's around 4.5% to 4.8%.
  • Floating-rate home loans currently charge 7.25% to 8.45%. Prepaying saves you that rate with no tax on the saving.
  • The RBI held rates at 5.25% for the fourth time in August 2026. Most economists don't expect another cut before 2027.
  • If your home loan rate is above 7.5%, prepaying beats an FD at any major bank after tax.
  • No home loan? Lock a two-year FD now. Waiting for rates to climb is probably a losing bet.

The RBI held its repo rate at 5.25% on August 5, and the message was clear: don't expect relief anytime soon. Four holds in a row. Most economists are penciling in a flat rate through the rest of 2026. So if you have extra cash sitting around, the question isn't whether rates will move. It's whether you're using that money well right now.

The answer depends almost entirely on one thing: whether you're carrying a floating-rate home loan.

What Does the RBI Rate Hold Mean for Your Money?

When the RBI holds rates, bank deposit and lending rates tend to drift sideways. FD rates at major banks have been easing since December 2025, when the repo was last cut from 5.5% to 5.25%. SBI now offers 6.45%, HDFC and ICICI at around 6.50%, and Kotak at 6.80% for two-year deposits. Some small finance banks still offer 8%, though those carry meaningfully higher credit risk.

This isn't the rate environment of 2023, when five-year FDs at major banks were routinely touching 7.5%. We're past that. Waiting for rates to climb back up is definately a mistake for most people.

What Is Your FD Actually Earning After Tax?

FD interest is taxable as ordinary income in India. In the 30% bracket, a 6.80% FD return comes out to about 4.76% after tax, and a 6.45% FD drops to roughly 4.5%. For someone in the 20% bracket, the numbers run from 5.1% to 5.4% after tax. These are decent returns for a near-zero-risk instrument, but not the whole story.

Compare that with what a floating-rate home loan is actually costing you.

Should You Prepay Your Home Loan Instead of Locking an FD?

If your home loan rate is above 7.5%, prepaying almost certainly beats any FD at a major bank after tax. Every rupee of principal you reduce saves you the loan rate with no TDS deducted and no income tax on the saving. That's a guaranteed 7.25% to 8.45% return the FD market can't match right now.

Here's why this matters. Say you're paying 8.25% on a repo-linked home loan and you put 2 lakh toward prepayment. You've effectively earned 8.25% on that money, risk-free. No FD at SBI or HDFC currently comes close to that after tax.

There are real exceptions. If your loan rate is below 7%, which applies to some older fixed-rate borrowers, the math gets closer. And if you're still claiming large deductions under Section 24b (home loan interest, up to 2 lakh per year) or Section 80C (principal repayment), calculate your actual after-deduction cost before prepaying. For borrowers deep into the loan term who are mainly paying principal, that deduction benefit has already shrunk anyway.

FD vs. Home Loan Prepayment: A Quick Comparison

OptionRateAfter 30% TaxLiquidity
SBI FD (2 years)6.45%~4.5%Low
Kotak FD (2 years)6.80%~4.76%Low
Small finance bank FD7.5-8.5%~5.3-6%Low-medium
Home loan prepayment7.25-8.45%7.25-8.45%*None

*Savings on home loan interest are not taxed as income, so the effective return equals the loan rate. Once prepaid, that money isn't accessible without taking a new loan.

When Does Locking an FD Still Make Sense?

An FD makes sense when you have no outstanding home loan or need savings you can access quickly. Senior citizens get an additional 0.5% from most banks, bringing Kotak's two-year rate to 7.30%, which is genuinely competitive right now.

It also works if you need the money within 12 months. A liquid mutual fund is slightly better on an after-tax basis for that window, but a short-term FD is fine if you prefer simplicity.

If you lock an FD, a two-year tenure makes more sense than five years right now. Rates aren't going up, and the next RBI move is almost certainly a cut, probably in early 2027. A two-year FD captures current rates without leaving you stuck through multiple rounds of easing.

One situation that's easy to miss: if you have both a home loan and spare savings but also need some liquidity, split the money. Put 60 to 70% toward prepayment and keep the rest in a short-term FD or liquid fund. Keeping these entirely seperate as decisions is where a lot of people leave money on the table quietly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will FD rates fall in 2026?

Probably not by much in the coming months. The RBI's August 2026 pause signals stability, and banks haven't been aggressively cutting deposit rates. That could change when the next repo rate cut arrives, which most forecasters now place in early 2027. Current FD rates are close to their ceiling for this rate cycle.

Is prepaying your home loan better than putting money in an FD?

For most borrowers with a floating-rate loan above 7.5%, yes. You save the loan rate after tax, which beats a major-bank FD on an after-tax basis right now. If your loan rate is below 7%, factor in remaining tax deductions before deciding.

Which bank offers the highest FD rate in August 2026?

Among large banks, Kotak Mahindra Bank offers 6.80% for two-year deposits, with 7.30% for senior citizens. Small finance banks can reach 8 to 8.5%, though at higher credit risk than a public sector or large private bank. Stable Money tracks current rates across institutions if you want a quick comparison.

Should you pick a 1-year or 2-year FD right now?

Two years is the better call for most people. One-year FDs mature into a likely lower-rate environment if the RBI cuts in early 2027. Five years locks you in through multiple potential changes. A two-year term captures the current rate without tying up your cash too long.

Does an RBI rate hold affect your existing FD?

No. A rate hold has no effect on FDs already booked. The rate you locked in stays fixed until maturity. Floating-rate home loans respond directly to the repo rate, so a hold also means your EMI stays unchanged too, for now.

The Short Version

If you carry a home loan above 7.5% and have spare cash, prepaying beats any major-bank FD after tax. No loan? Lock a two-year FD now rather than waiting for rates to rise. The RBI is on hold and the next move is almost certainly a cut. Act on that fact.

This is general financial information, not financial advice. For decisions specific to your situation, consider speaking with a fee-only financial planner.
